portfolio.label: Portfolio + technical blog
portfolio.desc: A clean personal site with 3–5 deep technical write-ups (not tutorials — your own builds, decisions, failures). You already have jonarthurito.tech; the gap is *content that proves you think*. Proves: communication + ownership. This is the page recruiters land on.

books.n: Add a writeup per flagship project below. The build IS the blog post.
Short, concrete, shows the messy middle. Recruiters love this style.

cli_tool.label: A real CLI tool (published)
cli_tool.desc: One genuinely useful command-line tool, packaged and published (npm / PyPI / crates.io / Homebrew), with a README, tests, and CI. You already forked Bagels-sync (TUI + S3 sync) — turn that instinct into something shipped under your name. Proves: you can finish and release.

books.n: How a good CLI should behave. Free.

oss_contrib.label: Merged OSS contribution
oss_contrib.desc: Get a non-trivial pull request merged into a project people actually use. Start with docs/bugfixes in a tool you already run (NixOS packages, an Astro plugin, a TUI). Proves: you can read a large unfamiliar codebase and ship inside someone else's standards — the #1 thing juniors lack.

books.n: Pick a repo you use daily; find a 'good first issue'.

shell.label: Build your own shell
shell.desc: A working Unix shell in C: parsing, fork/exec, pipes, redirection, job control, signals. ~2 weekends. Proves: you actually understand processes and the OS, not just `npm run`. The classic systems warm-up.

books.n: The canonical walkthrough. Then extend it past the tutorial.
The master list — your whole sys track lives here.

http_server.label: HTTP server from scratch
http_server.desc: An HTTP/1.1 server on raw sockets — no framework — handling concurrent connections (thread pool or epoll/async). In C or Go. Proves: you understand the network stack and concurrency from the bottom. Foundation for the backend track.

books.n: The sockets bible. Free.

books.t: CodeCrafters: Build your own HTTP server
books.n: Test-driven, language-agnostic stages.

interpreter.label: Interpreter (Crafting Interpreters)
interpreter.desc: A tree-walking interpreter for a small language (Lox): lexer, Pratt parser, environments, closures, classes. Proves: you grok how languages work — and it directly feeds your learning-rigorous compilers/type-theory nodes. One of the most respected solo projects.

books.n: Free online, flawless. Do Part II (jlox) end to end.

bytecode_vm.label: Bytecode VM + compiler
bytecode_vm.desc: Compile your language to bytecode and run it on a VM you write, with a garbage collector. Part III of Crafting Interpreters (clox, in C). Proves: real low-level chops — memory, dispatch, GC. Serious signal.

books.n: The hard, impressive half.

kv_store.label: Key-value store (Redis-lite)
kv_store.desc: An in-memory KV server speaking a simple TCP protocol (RESP), with a few data types and TTLs. Proves: protocols + concurrency + state. The gateway to the database and distributed tracks.

books.n: Step-by-step in C/C++.

storage_engine.label: Durable storage engine (WAL + LSM)
storage_engine.desc: Give your KV store an on-disk storage engine: write-ahead log, crash recovery, then an LSM-tree or Bitcask layout with compaction. Proves: you understand durability and the guts of every database. Rare in a junior portfolio.

books.n: Storage-engine bible; pairs with your DDIA reading.
A tiny, beautiful design you can implement in a weekend.

mini_sql.label: SQL query engine
mini_sql.desc: A small SQL engine over your storage engine: parser → logical plan → executor, with a couple of join algorithms and indexes. Proves: end-to-end database understanding. Ties to your learning-rigorous databases node.

books.t: Let's Build a Simple Database (sqlite clone)
books.n: Great on-ramp; then add SQL + joins.

raft_kv.label: Distributed KV with Raft
raft_kv.desc: Make your KV store fault-tolerant via Raft consensus: leader election, log replication, snapshots — survive node failures. THE distributed-systems flagship. Proves the exact thing your 'Distributed Application Architecture' coursework only described. Hireable on its own.

books.n: Do labs 2–4 (Raft → fault-tolerant KV). Public.

books.t: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)
books.n: The paper. Readable by design.

container_runtime.label: Mini container runtime
container_runtime.desc: A tiny Docker-like runtime: namespaces + cgroups + an overlay rootfs, in Go or C. ~300 lines for the core. Proves: you know what a container actually *is* (not magic). Great interview story.

books.n: Live-codes it in Go in 40 min. Reproduce + extend.

prod_api.label: Production-grade API service
prod_api.desc: A real backend: REST or gRPC, JWT/OAuth auth, Postgres with migrations, input validation, error handling, and a genuine test suite. Level up your Menyala IoT / Spring Boot intern work into something production-shaped. Proves: you can build the thing companies pay for.

books.n: The backend engineer's bible — also on your learning-rigorous list.

caching_queue.label: Caching + async job queue
caching_queue.desc: Add Redis caching (with invalidation), plus a background job queue and workers for slow tasks. Proves: you think about latency and decoupling — senior-flavored concerns in a junior portfolio.

books.n: Cache-aside, rate limiting, queues.

observability.label: Observability + load test (with numbers)
observability.desc: Instrument the API with metrics + tracing (Prometheus / Grafana / OpenTelemetry), then load-test it (k6/wrk) and WRITE UP the numbers — p99 latency, throughput, what you fixed. Proves: engineering maturity. The blog post writes itself.

books.n: Measure, break, fix, document the before/after.

ci_cd_deploy.label: CI/CD + containerized deploy
ci_cd_deploy.desc: Dockerize the service, build a GitHub Actions pipeline (test → build → push → deploy), and deploy it somewhere real (a VPS or your Pi). Proves: you can ship to production, not just to localhost.

books.n: You already use Docker — formalize it into a pipeline.

ml_from_scratch.label: Core ML from scratch (numpy)
ml_from_scratch.desc: Implement linear/logistic regression, an MLP, and backprop by hand in numpy — no framework. Then a tiny autograd engine. Proves: you understand ML, not just `model.fit()`. Feeds your learning-rigorous deep-learning node.

books.n: Build autograd + a transformer from zero. The single best ML-builder course. Free.

reproduce_paper.label: Reproduce a paper
reproduce_paper.desc: Pick one focused paper and reproduce its core result on a small dataset (a GPT from scratch, a diffusion toy model, a classic CV/NLP result). Proves: you can turn research into working code — exactly what ML roles screen for.

books.n: Reproduce a small GPT; document the loss curves.
Pick something with a public dataset you can run on a laptop/Colab.

ml_service.label: End-to-end ML service
ml_service.desc: Train a model, serve it behind an API, monitor it, and deploy it — the full MLOps loop. Combine your ML + backend tracks. Proves: you can ship ML to production, the rarest and most-hired ML skill.

books.n: End-to-end MLOps, free.

market_data.label: Market-data pipeline
market_data.desc: Ingest live + historical market data (crypto exchange APIs are free and need no broker), normalize it, and store ticks/bars efficiently. Proves: data engineering + the substrate for everything quant. Cheap to start, today.

books.n: Free unified access to 100+ exchanges. Start with Binance/Bybit public feeds.

backtester.label: Event-driven backtesting engine
backtester.desc: A backtester that replays data event-by-event (no look-ahead bias) with realistic fills, fees, and slippage. Proves: you understand market mechanics and can build correct simulations. The core quant-dev tool.

books.n: Build it event-driven from the start — vectorized backtests lie.

strategy.label: A strategy with honest metrics
strategy.desc: Implement a couple of strategies and report them HONESTLY: Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, after fees + slippage. Proves: intellectual honesty about edge — the trait quant firms actually test for. Most candidate strategies are overfit; show you know that.

books.n: Especially the chapters on backtest overfitting and why most edges are fake.

lob_sim.label: Limit order book + matching engine
lob_sim.desc: A full limit-order-book with a price-time-priority matching engine. Proves: you understand microstructure at the data-structure level. Directly maps to your learning-rigorous market-microstructure node.

books.t: How to Build a Fast Limit Order Book
books.n: The canonical design; intrusive linked lists + price-level map.

lowlat_cpp.label: Low-latency C++ order book
lowlat_cpp.desc: Rebuild the order book in modern C++ obsessed with latency: cache-friendly layout, no allocations on the hot path, lock-free where it counts — and BENCHMARK it (ns/op, p99). THE HFT flagship, and it leans straight on your C++ + competitive-programming strengths. This single repo can get you HFT interviews.

books.t: CppCon talks: 'When a Microsecond Is an Eternity'
books.n: How HFT C++ actually thinks. Then measure everything.

books.t: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory
books.n: Cache behavior is the whole game here.

pi_selfhost.label: Self-host on the Raspberry Pi 5
pi_selfhost.desc: Your first tinker: set up the Pi 5, run Docker on it, and self-host one real service you actually use (a bookmark manager, an RSS reader, your reading-tracker-api). Expose it safely (Tailscale/Cloudflare Tunnel). Proves: you can run real infra. Turns the Pi from a drawer object into a lab.

books.n: Start here — one service, end to end, this weekend.
Pick something you'll genuinely use.

pi_monitoring.label: Homelab monitoring stack
pi_monitoring.desc: Run Prometheus + Grafana on the Pi and graph the Pi itself + your self-hosted services. Proves: ops instinct, and gives you the observability muscle the backend track needs.

books.n: Node exporter → dashboards → an alert that fires.

pi_k3s.label: k3s cluster + GitOps
pi_k3s.desc: Run lightweight Kubernetes (k3s) on the Pi and deploy your own apps to it via GitOps (Argo CD / Flux). Proves: you can operate the orchestration layer every backend shop uses. Combine with your CI/CD project for a deploy-to-cluster story.

books.n: Even a single-node cluster teaches the whole model.

pi_embedded.label: Embedded / bare-metal on the Pi
pi_embedded.desc: Talk to hardware: GPIO, a sensor (temp/camera/distance), maybe an interrupt-driven loop or a Pico for true bare-metal. Builds directly on your II2260 Embedded Systems course (your ⭐4 repo). Proves: you cross the hardware/software line — rare and memorable.

books.t: Raspberry Pi Pico C/C++ SDK / gpiozero
books.n: Start with a sensor; graph its readings in your monitoring stack.

pi_edge_ml.label: Edge ML on the Pi
pi_edge_ml.desc: Run one of your trained models on the Pi against a live camera/mic feed (quantized / ONNX runtime). Combines ML + infra + embedded into one striking demo. Proves: the full stack from model to metal.

books.t: ONNX Runtime / TFLite on Raspberry Pi
books.n: A real-time inference demo videos beautifully for your portfolio.
